utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The delay is due largely to me. I must apologise. A meeting I was in went longer and everything was pushed back. I understand there may be some short matter to be raised. Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't heard from you for a week.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it's that time. Your Honours may be aware that the joint Defence response to the Prosecution's motion on the admission of Ramadan Behluli's prior statement was due yesterday after a kind extension of time to yesterday. Your Honour, there is work underway in terms of agreeing a joint Defence position to present to the Trial Chamber so the Trial Chamber only have to deal with one document as opposed to three separate documents and three different teams. That would take approximately one more week to complete. I've spoken to my learned friend Mr. Whiting from the Prosecution who has indicated that from their point of view they would have not concerns about an extension of one week of time to the Defence, and my application now is for a further week to prepare such a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have the week, Mr. Powles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POWLES
utterances.text: I'm very grateful, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That a week from today or a week from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: A week from when it was spoken would be the normal, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's and extra day that's being cribbed. I recognise your own point, Mr. Whiting: It means you're owed one. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're owed one?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's right. I'm just trying to bank the credit for future use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It has been mentioned to me that there is some occasion to mark the International Women's Day and that it would be perhaps convenient if people were able to attend that. I do not know whether it will prove practical in the flow of the evidence today for that to occur, but it will be kept in our mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's at what time, Your Honour, if I may, that event?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The registry officer knows exactly. I think it was 5.30. Would that be confirmed? That can be confirmed during the course of the afternoon. Mr. Buja, good afternoon. If I could remind you of the affirmation you took at the beginning of your evidence which still applies. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, are you able to hear and understand me clearly?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I want to carry on from an answer that you gave at the end of the day yesterday in response to a question that I put to you about the diagram that you drew in the interview that you had with the Office of the Prosecutor in 2003. And what you said is, and I'm going to just read it from the transcript, you said -- you said: "I'm saying that through Jakup Krasniqi we were conveyed orders by the General Staff. He was the only member of the General Staff that we knew and through which we could take orders of the General Staff." Now, what I'm going to suggest to you through my questions, Mr. Buja, is that what you have done is you have changed your story and you have inserted Jakup Krasniqi here in the place where you previously had Fatmir Limaj. And what I'm going to do is I'm going to go to the first part of your interview with the Office of the Prosecutor where you began the story with your arrival with Fatmir Limaj in Drenica in March of 1998, and I'm going to show to you parts of the transcript about those matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if the transcript could be provided to the witness. And for the record the diagram -- the diagram that was being referenced yesterday is U003-3675 is also being put before the witness. I would draw the witness's attention to page 22 of the Albanian and in the English it's page 23 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, at the bottom -- at the bottom of page 22 of the Albanian, do you see the question: "When you arrived in Drenica, were you still together as a group of 30 people until the moment when you arrived in Drenica?" Do you see that question? It's the last question. Do you see that, sir, that question at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, even though before that in -- during the proofing I already explained that I cannot come up with a statement that I'm seeing for the first time here and that I suspected that manipulations were made. I suspected about the veracity of the translation, and especially it seemed to me kind of blackmail on the part of Ole Lehtinen when he didn't enable me to see it, knowing that the statements are usually translated, as the case was in the Milosevic trial when I had to meet three times with the Prosecutors and amend -- improve the statement three times because of the mistakes made by the translators. This is why I demanded that this statement be given to me so that I make the necessary improvements. Now that I see the statement it doesn't make any sense to me because I see many mistakes, many misinterpretations which might be due to poor translation. So I would ask this Trial Chamber to interrupt this procedure of facing me -- of putting me the statement which I do not consider valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, first of all I want to explain to you that the transcript that you have before you is the -- the Albanian words that you -- that were put to you during the interview and the Albanian words that you spoke during the interview. So there is no issue about translation, and the rest of us have a translation of the words in Albanian that were put to you and the words in Albanian that you spoke. Now, if you could just simply answer my questions and you'll have an opportunity to explain these parts of the interview. And I'm -- so that there's no question about the translation or the circumstances of -- circumstances of the interview or the questions, I'm going to play the interview for you. Now, starting at this page at the bottom of page 22, I'm going to play this portion of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "O.L.: When you arrived in Drenica, the group of 30 persons were still together. Is that correct? "S.B.: Yes, the group was -- there was 30 members of the group, 'til the arrival in Drenica. Yeah, in Drenica, we were assigned to private houses. On our arrival there we were assigned to private houses. Yeah, we've spent days there. I don't know how many days, but we stayed definitely for several days. And then an order was issued that we had to go to this area, including Malisheve, Suhareke" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the other named places. I can't -- "S.B.: So it was about the area outside Drenica. "O.L.: During the time in Drenica, were you informed about the organisation and division of the KLA at that time? "S.B.: We only -- we had no possibility to get informed. At that time UCK had very limited scope of activity, but it's -- I'm by nature not curious. As a person being in prison, I knew from my experience that. "O.L.: Who was the one giving the order for you to go to this area? "S.B.: Well, I don't know who is the person who issued the orders, but who conveyed this order to me was Hashim Thaqi. "O.L.: Okay. And did Hashim Thaqi tell you that Fatmir Limaj is the one who is going to be the commander of this unit going to the area? "S.B.: Well, no, but we knew that Fatmir Limaj -- we knew Fatmir Limaj was a more competent person in terms that he knew -- he knew -- he knew the terrain better than the others. Fatmir Limaj was assigned to coordinate the things in -- with the general headquarters. And my task was to coordinate things with Fatmir. "Right, it was -- it was a sort of -- if the -- if -- the moment would come of starting setting up units or other forms of military organisations, I would relate to Fatmir and then Fatmir to the general headquarters, and then back to -- this way back."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I want to go through point by point that part of the interview. You said at the beginning that when you arrived in Drenica you were still together, a group of 30 people. That's correct, isn't it? You were approximately 30 people when you arrived in Drenica?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have said this and I'm saying this again to the Trial Chamber that we were about 30 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you -- the next thing you say is that you spread out among the houses, and that's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we spread out among the houses in the villages that I mentioned to this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were there for several days, and that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were given an order to leave and organise in areas of Suhareke, Malisevo, Lipjan, Stimlje, Prizren, Kacanik, and that's also correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it cannot be correct because the term "order" has been wrongly used, as you already mentioned to me because at that time we didn't get orders from anyone. I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you used the word "order" in the transcript -- in the interview, didn't you? You said: "We were given the order." Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is why I'm saying -- I mean the mistakes that I might have made during the interviewing. I demanded that the fair procedure, the normal procedure, be used in my case, that is I should be given the transcript just for me to go over it and see what mistakes I may have made. I had to recollect events which have taken place five, six years ago. It was a hard task for me to recollect all those things in the form they happened at that time. It was later that I realised that -- the words that I -- were conveyed to me by the General Staff, I interpreted them as orders, but in fact they were not orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, between yesterday and today, have you talked with anybody about your testimony here today, about your testimony here at the Tribunal between yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have talked about the testimony, but I didn't go into details as what exactly we talked here. I called my family, my brother, and my wife telling that I am okay and the trial is going on. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did anybody tell you to come in here and say that you wanted to have your transcript and go over it and make changes, the way you have suggested today? Did anybody say that to you between yesterday and today?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have constantly demanded to be given the transcript by Ole Lehtinen so that I could correct the mistakes. You know very well that even during proofing I was not given the transcript. We only talked briefly together and that I have already pointed out that -- with an interview recorded which -- whose text I didn't see, to find out any possible mistakes I cannot sit here and tell the truth as I am supposed to do under oath. I am here under oath and I have to say as they truly were. This has tormented me for a long time, that is to recollect events as they truly were and not as they were after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you're going to -- I'm going to give you an opportunity here to go through important parts of your transcript and if you have explanations or want to correct mistakes, you can do that. So you have said that you were not given an order in fact. Can Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you explain to me how it is that you said during the interview that you were given an order to organise these various areas. Can you explain how you made that mistake, if it was a mistake.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I can explain it. I spoke, as many others do, in interviews on the basis of what we found out later, that is on the basis of the people whom we knew later whose words we took for orders by the General Staff. At that time I didn't know that Hashim Thaqi was a member of the General Staff. It was later during the war and especially after the war that I knew him to be a member of the General Staff. So this is where the mistake may have occurred. This explained why I perceived it as an order instead of putting it in the context of the time and the circumstances of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So what you're saying is that at the time you didn't think it was an order but later you realised that it was an order. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later I interpreted it as an order, even though at the time it was given it was not given to us in the form of an order. It was not -- we were not told that Hashim Thaqi is a member of the General Staff; it is said that he is a man who has links, connections, with the General Staff. You have to understand that in the period we are talking about and even at a later time the members of the General Staff were in profound illegality. No one knew who the members of the General Staff were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I raise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Mansfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: May I raise a matter. I'm obliged. I think we're very concerned about what the witness is saying concerning his request to have a copy of the transcript of the interview which took place some time ago now, 2003, about events that took place even longer ago than that. It is a matter of course that was part of the submissions that we made to Your Honour, and I don't know of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you're thinking of putting it again, we've considered it and it is our view that the course of the examination and cross-examination will -- in the ordinary way deal adequately with that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It's a slight, if I may put it, refinement on that, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It had better be a markedly different refinement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: It's merely a question of fairness that in most cases in fact --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're very conscious of fairness and we've thought about this quite a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: And it is -- normally a witness will have had a copy -- whoever they are, they will have had a copy before they give their evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The problem is not that the witness doesn't remember or is confused about that; the issue is whether he used words or not, whether they were put to him by others rather than himself and so on. And we think what is being manifested here is one that is not going to be assisted by an opportunity to go through the statement and identify errors on his own. If there are errors, they will be identified in the course of those matters being put to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I can't take the matter further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your testimony is that you did not know at the time that Hashim Thaqi was a member of the General Staff. Right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But Hashim Thaqi told you to go and organise those areas, Suva Reka, Malisevo, Lipjan, Shtime, and so forth. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told that we had to go to these places where there were not yet guerrilla units, as I mentioned Suhareke, Malisheve, Stimlje, Prizren, and Kacanik. And I have already explained even earlier that I had demanded to be posted in areas of Shtime and Lipjan, whose territory I knew very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you say this was communicated by Hashim Thaqi. You say that in the interview, and that's correct, right? And then you say -- you say: "Fatmir Limaj was assigned the task of coordinating work with the General Staff while I had to coordinate with Fatmir. That is in fact how the organisation would work, because there had not been any organisation for some time, that is any organisation of units. An information had to be brought to Fatmir, and then from Fatmir to the General Staff and they -- we -- could then come back to us with what we had to do next." And that is what happened, isn't it? Fatmir --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. At this time I'm going to object to any question because it's compound. He already has asked for an answer with regard to receiving information from Hashim Thaqi; he has not received an answer to that question. We are now moving on. Because of the delicate nature of what we're dealing with I think it's important that we get answers to any question asked and we do not have more than one question compounded at any one time to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's entirely a sensible proposition, Mr. Guy-Smith. There may be occasions when it appears to the questioner at the end of a question that what he said isn't clear and he goes on to make it more clear, and I think you have been very skilful in managing to incorrect any imperfections in your first question that way. If that occurs, it would not be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me break this up a little bit. You have told us that this was communicated -- the instruction to go organise those areas was communicated by Hashim Thaqi, and that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Certainly. The -- you have already told us that Hashim Thaqi was the one who communicated to you the instruction -- who told you to go organise those areas. Right? Suva Reka, Lipjan, Malisevo, that came from Hashim Thaqi. Right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instructions were given to me to go to Lipjan and Shtime. In the case of Malisheve he asked Fatmir Limaj to go. In the case of Suhareke it was thought that Kumanova should go. For Kacanik it was Agim Bajrami who went.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you say "he," this is Hashim Thaqi that we're talking about. Right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then you say in the interview, you say, and I will read it and then I will ask you questions. You say: "Fatmir Limaj was assigned the task of coordinating work with the General Staff, while I had to coordinate with Fatmir. That is in fact how the organisation would work because there had not been any organisation for some time, that is any organisation of units, an information had to be brought from Fatmir and then from Fatmir to the General Staff and they -- we -- could then come back to us with what we had to do next." Now, it's true, isn't it, that Fatmir Limaj was assigned the task of coordinating work with the General Staff. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a very major mistake because in fact Fatmir Limaj wasn't given the task to coordinate the work with the General Staff as it is said here. Fatmir Limaj had to coordinate my trips and I had to coordinate Agim Bajrami's trip to the General Staff. It was this coordination that we had to do to arrive in Drenica where we had met Hashim Thaqi even earlier. This was a form of organisation then, until May, when I undertook to coordinate the unit -- the operation of units in Kacanik, Lipjan, Shtime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, can you explain -- these are your words from the interview. This is you speaking when you say: "Fatmir Limaj was assigned the task of coordinating work with the General Staff." Can you explain how you made that mistake when you were being interviewed?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made this mistake because I thought that the word "coordinate" covered actions that had to have been carried out by Fatmir Limaj in the -- because the territory where he was located was closer to Drenica compared to the place where we were. And the territory where I operated was closer compared to that where Agim Bajrami was operating. So in order to coordinate the work with the General Staff, Agim Bajrami had to come to me and I was -- took measures to ensure his trip to Fatmir and then Fatmir would take care of the part of the trip to Drenice. So the word "coordinate" or "coordination" meant this, that is the form of escort. But this is why it has been misunderstood probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, Mr. Buja, that's not what you say when you explain your answer because what you say is: "This is how the organisation would work: Information had to be brought to Fatmir and from Fatmir to the General Staff, and they would come back with what we had to do next." So what you say is information was transmitted to the General Staff through Fatmir Limaj and instructions on what you had to do next would be transmitted from the General Staff back through -- through Fatmir Limaj to you. That's what you say, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that this is written so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you explain to me, sir, how you made that mistake. If that's a mistake, how is it possible that you said that? Can you explain why you said that if it's not in fact the truth?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a piece of information, I cannot explain to you why I gave it. Because even at the time of the interview I was studying journalism, and the way I understood the meaning of the word "information" is a simple piece of information. And I don't understand why it's been used in this way. What I know is I recollect events very well and I clearly underline the form of coordination of events of operations among us. And I want to explain to you that I'm telling the truth and I'm giving you an example that I was appointed commander of the subzone. If Fatmir Limaj was at a higher level as you are claiming here, how can it be that he wouldn't be appointed at least commander of a subzone? It means as if I was the commander of my commander; it doesn't make sense, this form of organisation you are claiming has existed then, as if Fatmir Limaj was my superior. Even during proofing I explained that Fatmir Limaj has never been my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, we're talking about a period in March and April and May and June before you were appointed to the command of the subzone of Nerodimlje. Now, you -- when you gave this interview to the OTP, you had already testified in this courtroom in another case, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you have told us now that you recollect events very well and that you were studying journalism at the time you gave this interview with the OTP. That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it your testimony that you have no explanation -- you cannot give us an explanation for why it is you said here that that is how the organisation would work: Information would be brought to Fatmir and passed to the General Staff and then instructions on what you should do would come from the General Staff through Fatmir back to you? Are you saying you cannot now give us an explanation for why you said that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, before this trial I explained clearly the form of organisation we had. I have explained up to what time, and that is until the end of April it wasn't possible for me to contact Fatmir Limaj. And the form of organisation that is described here could not have existed because it was impossible for me to go to Fatmir Limaj until April, end of April 1998, and my contact with Fatmir Limaj at that time, the purpose of this meeting was not to contact the General Staff but to contact Hashim Thaqi who I thought was in Drenica, could be found in Drenica --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I'm going to interrupt your answer because I think you're repeating what you said before and you're not answering my question. My question is: If this is not in fact the truth, what you describe here in your OTP interview about the structure, then why did you say it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand why it was said in this way, simply because for some time I had to think about this. At the time when I gave this interview I thought a little about those events hoping that we will have the chance to check these documents and make the corrections, the necessary corrections in these documents. I hoped that after my meeting with the investigator in Milosevic's case when I was told that I will be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. given the opportunity to correct -- to make the necessary corrections, and simply without paying much attention I gave an interview thinking that I will have a chance to make corrections. Now you are using this in order to put me in a not very desirable situation. I am clearly stating here in this trial the form of organisation we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, it's not a very desirable situation because what you said in your OTP interview is the truth, isn't it? Isn't that why it's not a very desirable situation?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not in a situation to say until today to the Office of the Prosecutor whether it was true or not true because I didn't have this statement. And here I am telling the truth because I am under oath, and I made it clear to you without seeing this statement beforehand, it isn't possible for me to claim whether it is true or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, in this interview that was recorded over several hours, did you ever ask for the opportunity to review the transcript or ever indicate that you had not -- were not clear about your answers or you wanted to correct mistakes? Did you ever say that during the interview?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the interview, I clearly told you that some things were made clear but not everything and that additional clearing is necessary because it had been some time since those events had happened. I believed in the honesty of the OTP after the contact I had with the investigator Ole Lehtinen and the investigator in Milosevic's case, who explained to me that the procedure will be the same. I believed that this was the procedure that was going to be applied in this case. After my meeting with Ole Lehtinen, I asked for the transcript because I thought that mistakes could have happened. I asked for this transcript even later when I contacted again Ole Lehtinen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Since you've brought up your meetings with Ole Lehtinen, isn't it the case that when Ole Lehtinen later contacted you to be a witness in the trial, you refused to be a witness? You refused to come and testify? Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is completely true because I could not come to this trial and testify about something that I hadn't seen beforehand. Therefore, I asked Ole Lehtinen to give me the transcript, but it wasn't given to me. I suspected that my interview could have misused by this investigator [as interpreted]. I surely wanted to contact the Defence to clarify the possible misinterpretations. Ole Lehtinen clearly told me on the phone when I phoned him -- actually, he phoned me in order to schedule a contact. I told him that it would be possible to meet the next day. After ten minutes of this conversation, he called me again and asked for an urgent meeting because I was going to meet the Defence. I told him clearly -- I told Mr. Lehtinen clearly that I am giving a statement, a voluntary statement, and I don't have to render account to anyone. He told me that I should not go to this meeting. The next day he called and he apologised because he said it was a -- something -- a misinterpretation by the interpreter. I then conveyed my criticism to him for in a way ordering me by phone not to go and give a statement to the Defence; therefore, I refused to become a witness for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, isn't it in fact the case that you came to the ICTY office in Pristina and told Mr. Lehtinen that you did not want to be a witness in this trial because you were afraid? Isn't that in fact what happened?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was not the meeting we had with Mr. Lehtinen, but it was a meeting that we had with Ole Lehtinen and you, Mr. Prosecutor, where I clearly put it before you that I do not want to become a Prosecution witness and I didn't want to be misunderstood from my own population. Because the statement might be misinterpreted by the population, and therefore I didn't want to be part here as part of the Prosecution. I did in fact respect the subpoena and came here because as Ole Lehtinen said, if I did not obey and respect this subpoena I could be arrested and punished. I told you that I was not concerned about the consequences for me as an individual, regardless of the punishment because these would be individual consequences and -- that would not involve my family and the entire Kosovo. This is what I said clearly during that meeting where you attended as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And isn't it in fact true that Mr. Lehtinen never told you not to go to an interview with the Defence? He never said that to you, did he?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through the phone, meaning through the interpreter who translated Mr. Lehtinen's words, I was told that we should meet and not to go and give a statement or interview to the Defence. This is true and I can testify about this. The Defence, when I went to see them, I explained to them clearly the way I was told by the phone [as interpreted] through the interpreter who was interpreting Mr. Lehtinen's words.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, you went to an interview with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the interview with the Defence, did you review your transcript of your interview with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in contact with the Defence, and they explained my interview and they said that if I gave a statement for the Defence, that statement would be recorded and then would be given to me so that I could check possible mistakes. And after reviewing the statement, then I would be able to sign it. This is a form of interview that was -- that I was familiar with even during my experience with the OTP. Therefore --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja -- Mr. Buja, I'm going to interrupt you. My question is: During your interview with the Defence, did you review your transcript of your interview with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the interview with the Defence, I did not have the opportunity to see this transcript, the OTP transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you see any transcript of your interview with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the meeting the following day, meaning after the meeting with the Defence, when I met with the OTP and after my remarks that I presented to Mr. Ole Lehtinen, he brought me five CDs which I was never able to open. I even attempted to open these CDs by the help of experts, computer experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These CDs contained the transcript of your interview with the OTP, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had requested the transcripts, both from my statement in Milosevic case and this one. I wanted to have all the recordings and all the transcripts, so I was given five disks. I tried to open the five of them and I did not manage, even by the help of some experts who were my soldiers in the past.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Buja, did you ever contact Mr. Lehtinen to tell him that you were unable to open those disks?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not contact Mr. Lehtinen because I thought at that time and I am convinced even today that the attention was to manipulate with my statement and therefore I did not want to contact Mr. Lehtinen because of these reasons. Other reasons for me not to contact the OTP are: In March last year I was arrested for the March events under an indictment where it is stated that I violated 1244 Resolution and that although there wasn't any base for that. During this detention I was visited by the Prosecution, who explained to me that a letter had been sent by the Prosecution to the commander, a KFOR commander, in which it said that I was sincere and I had given a statement in Milosevic trial and that I was going to testify for crimes committed by Albanians. I had never said such a thing and I did not have this conviction that Albanians committed any crimes. This letter which arrived 15 days after my detention, two days after it was received I was released and I interpreted as a way how the OTP had force in power in Kosovo, and I interpreted it as a blackmail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After you -- after you were released was when you told the OTP that in fact you would not be a witness in the Prosecution -- in the trial, isn't it? You told the Prosecution that you would not be a witness. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You said that in the March events you were arrested and held for a certain time by KFOR, and my question is: Wasn't it after you were released that you told the Prosecution you would not in fact be a witness in the trial? Isn't that true? In the fall of last year you told the Prosecution you would not be a witness.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that this happened in March last year, this letter, and the meeting with Ole Lehtinen took place later. And the phone call from Ole Lehtinen of course made me even more suspicious in the OTP intentions to misuse my interpret -- my interview. After the call when Ole Lehtinen told me that I would receive this transcript and the intention to accuse these people who I know that did not commit any crime and that are not guilty, during that time that we had this meeting I made it clear that I have a high esteem for these sons here and I am convinced that they did not commit any crimes. I consider the KLA warfare as a very fair one and a clear one, a pure one. I made it clear through the entire time of my interview that the KLA did not commit crimes. And you later -- or sorry, Ole Lehtinen later insisted that I should admit that mistakes might have happened. And my answer was clear, that mistakes might have happened and even mistakes might have happened on behalf of NATO during the bombing campaign. I was not given an opportunity to correct any possible mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, by virtue of the witness's answer, I don't know whether or not such a letter is in the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor; however, I would request on the behalf of the Defence that we receive a copy of any letters that may exist in this regard. I also would request at this time that we receive any notes, memorandum, or any memorialisations that exist with regard to any conversations or contact Mr. Lehtinen had with this particular witness during this particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to the letter, I believe it's been disclosed, but if it hasn't I can certainly make sure that it has been. I can check if there are any notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could let Mr. Guy-Smith know in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I'm going to take you -- since you have said - you have said repeatedly - how you thought the interview would work and that you wanted to have an interview to review it, I'm going to take you to the end of the interview and see what you say at the end of the interview. In your version it's on page 104 in Albanian and in English it's page 86. It starts -- on page 104 it starts about a third of the way down and I'm going to play it for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "A.W.: This time period, the spring and summer 1998, about this area, about Lapusnik. You've told us what you do know; you've told us things that you don't know. Is there anything else that you think is important about the things that we've talked about that we should know or have we covered everything? "S.B.: I believe most of the -- we've covered most of the issues, although I might -- I might -- it's pretty hard to understand -- to understand that period. It's hard to have a comprehensive view about the form of organisations about -- because of the mess at that time -- well, some things are beginning to sorted out -- to be clear -- well, I can say that generally speaking you must have -- you must have a clear view or -- about things now -- by now. Yeah, if there's something unclear to you, then I'll -- I'm always available at any time you need to get in touch with me to clarify the point or the issue that's unclear to you. "A.W.: Okay. That actually leads to my next question which is: If you were called to be a witness in The Hague, would you be willing to tell the Court everything you've told us today? "S.B.: The position of a witness is a bit sensitive -- difficult, but what I've declared here today so I would declare them openly and with no hesitation, publicly. But you must understand what's also my position. So I wouldn't prefer to be put in a difficult position. Yeah, well, on the fact of being called as a witness to testify in a case against my former comrades-in-arms puts me into a very difficult position, but I'm willing at any moment because I've made up my mind to be as transparent as possible, as open as possible, and I don't think it will be a big problem for me to come -- to come over there and to testify what I've testified today to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, do you see there at the end of the interview that you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. said: "In general things have been clarified." Do you see that you said that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that in general it was clarified but not everything was clarified. There was space for possible mistake because here the OTP will -- stuck on a word. Let's say as I earlier said about that information and therefore we needed to correct these mistakes. I said that I was ready to testify although the position of a witness, the very presence here even without talking before the comrades-in-arms who I believe are innocent -- I say it again here that things in general have been clarified but still there have been things that were not clear. And it is -- it can be clearly seen during this interview now that we played. And as I said, I believed we would have the possibility to make the necessary corrections and I expected this to happen, but it never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, you have stated that many, many times; I don't think you need to say it again. But isn't the reason that you are changing your story here not -- isn't it -- it's not because there were mistakes or misunderstandings; it's because you believe these men to be innocent and it is difficult to come here to give evidence against the men you fought with. Is that why -- isn't that the reason you are giving a different account here today about the structure?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not a different story, and this Chamber can investigate this statement even by means of other witnesses who I have mentioned in this interview. My difficulty was to be a Prosecution witness and the most difficult part was at that time and even today I was convinced that these boys are innocent and I cannot act and state things that were not true of that time. I stated clearly that I cannot be a person who through this statement given without thinking twice about the events that happened in April, May, and June. As for these events they were all like a story in themselves, and it is a pity that they're misinterpreted and put in a different form. And it's a pity that there was not a possibility for them to be clarified. I said that I was ready to give a statement when I would be able to correct that statement, make clear things that were not clear, and come as such before this trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's continue and see if we can get some further clarification. I'm going to ask you to turn to page 33 in the Albanian of the transcript, and I'm going to submit to you, sir, that it's not a matter of a word or a matter of misunderstanding but in fact, as I stated at the beginning of your testimony today, you have changed your account of the structure and you have now put Jakup Krasniqi in the place where you previously put Fatmir Limaj. And it's page 33 in the English at the top of the page and on the Albanian it's about a third of the way down the page on 33. And I'm going to play this portion of the tape which pertains -- you talking about May and June of 1998 when you're in the area -- you're working in the area of Kacanik, Ferizaj, and Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "O.L.: To collect weapons? "S.B.: These sort of activities were conducted in the period of May/June. It was during that time that a corridor was created from Albania to Kosovo. At that time my position consisted in being a coordinator for the area covering Kacanik, Ferizaj, Shtime. So I would coordinate -- I was coordinating things in connection with Limaj, who was placed in Klecka at that time."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you've already said in the interview, and we've spent some time on it, you've said that the -- that -- that Fatmir Limaj when you left -- when you arrived in Drenica that Fatmir Limaj was -- in March, that Fatmir Limaj was assigned to be the point between you and the General Staff, that you would send information up to the General Staff and instructions would come back down. Now, here you're talking about how things worked in May and June of 1998 when you were a coordinator of activity in the area of Kacanik. And you say that "my coordination was with Fatmir Limaj who was established in Klecka." Do you see that? Do you see where you say that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was true, wasn't it? When you were coordinating those activities in the area of Kacanik, Ferizaj, and Stimlje, you were coordinating with Fatmir Limaj, who was established in Klecka. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In June I already explained that the spokesperson of the KLA appeared in public as a member of the General Staff. It seems illogical at that time when I could contact Jakup Krasniqi to contact instead Fatmir Limaj. Why should I? The public appearance of Krasniqi as a member of the General Staff made it possible not only for me but for all the guerrilla units to contact the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir -- sir, let's talk about before that happened, before the 14th of June, 1998. Here you're talking about May and June when you're in Kacanik, Ferizaj, and Stimlje. And it says you coordinated with Fatmir Limaj, and that's true, isn't it, that you coordinated with Fatmir Limaj?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained this issue much earlier. It was in May 1998 that I was appointed by Hashim Thaqi to coordinate the operations of units in Kacanik, Ferizaj, Shtime, and Lipjan. This was an extra supplementary task given to me apart from the duty I had to coordinate the work for the supply line. It was at the end of May when I returned to Kroimire when the first unit was formed. Right after that I went back to Kacanik. Given the great need for armaments and supply in June, I didn't have any need at all after my return to contact Fatmir Limaj in the sense of organisation that you put me here. In June I contacted only Jakup Krasniqi. And my contacts with Fatmir Limaj in May and early June couldn't be possible because at that time I was in Kacanik and Ferizaj area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If that is true, then can you explain for us, please, why it is that you said in the interview that you -- your coordination was with Fatmir Limaj who was established in Klecka. You weren't -- that wasn't put to you; you said it yourself. Can you explain why you said that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meaning of the word "coordination," I think I explained it earlier. By this word "coordination" I understood the action to contact the General Staff and that Fatmir Limaj was supposed to make this contact possible. In June it wasn't necessary for Fatmir Limaj to do that, to escort me to the General Staff because by that time I could contact the member of the General Staff himself, who had just given a public interview in Klecka.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Fatmir Limaj's job when he was coordinating was not simply to show you the way to Drenica, but it was to be the -- a contact point with the General Staff. You could give information to the General Staff through Fatmir Limaj and get instructions from the General Staff through Fatmir Limaj. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already explained that this was not so because coordination had another meaning, not the meaning of hierarchy but the meaning of the operation, that is for me to contact the General Staff, as Agim Bajrami did, too. But my contacts with the General Staff were established in June when I returned from Kacanik, that is with Jakup Krasniqi. I am repeating here --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So -- and there's no need to repeat, sir. But is it your testimony then when you -- then that when you said here in the interview that: "My coordination was with Fatmir Limaj who was established at Klecka," is that what you are trying to say there is that -- is that Fatmir Limaj's role was to show you the way to Drenica if you wanted to meet with Hashim Thaqi? Is that what you're saying? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm putting it to you that the task of Fatmir Limaj at that time vis-a-vis myself was that from Klecka he should show me the way to Drenica, should accompany me to Drenica because that was an area that he knew well. It was the area he was born in. That's why we did -- this action was done; that is, I had to pass through this territory to Drenica where I always hoped to contact the members of the General Staff even though this never happened, because I didn't go to Drenica either in April, May, or June. But in June I managed to contact Jakup Krasniqi who was a public figure then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So -- in fact what you're saying here today now is that when you were organising in the area of Kacanik, Ferizaj, and Stimlje, you did not coordinate with Fatmir Limaj? That's your testimony now, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not coordinate with Fatmir Limaj because most of this time, that is March, April, I spent in Mullapolc. After my first attempt to contact with the members of the General Staff which failed, I returned again to Mullapolc to organise together with Imri Ilazi the unit in Ferizaj -- in order to enable me to go to Agim Bajrami and for Agim Bajrami to come to me. That period was the period when we didn't this form of have organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if the truth is that you did not coordinate with Fatmir Limaj, then I'm going to ask you again: Why did you say in the interview that you did coordinate with Fatmir Limaj? "My coordination was with Fatmir Limaj." Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I explained even earlier that the form of coordination was in the sense of coordination of the efforts to go to Drenice. This is why I mentioned the word "coordination"; this is what I had in mind, not something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you say that at the time in the interview? Did you say that that's what you meant?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the interview I didn't make any necessary explanations in the hope that things could be clarified at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure what the schedule is for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a convenient time, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, just quickly before the witness is brought in, I would just like to put on the record that the Prosecution located and disclosed notice of investigator Ole Lehtinen pertaining to meetings with Shukri Buja, as requested by the Defence. The letter that was referenced certainly exists; I thought it had been disclosed. We can't seem to put our hands on it at the moment, but we're working on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOPOLSKI
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder if I could just ask, forgive me, whether the document that has just been handed over which is headed "Investigator's Note" purports to be a contemporary document or one that has been helpfully but more recently compiled from other material.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's -- I'm almost certain, it was prepared in the last day or two and I think it's a contemporary document, prepared within days of the events described in the document, but that is also something I'll confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I've had an opportunity to get some notes pertaining to your meetings with Mr. Lehtinen. I want to ask you a few further questions about those matters, if I may. Isn't it the case that after your meeting with the Defence -- your interview with the Defence that you met with Mr. Lehtinen and you discussed with him what he had told you before the meeting with the Defence and you agreed with him that there had been a misunderstanding, that he had not in fact told you not to meet with the Defence but that there had been a misunderstanding on that subject? Isn't that what happened?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that there was a misunderstanding and a misinterpretation by the interpreter, and that day that interpreter was not present at the meeting with Ole Lehtinen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And isn't it true that you could not remember what had been said to you, the exact wording of what had been said to you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered how the interpreter put it, but it seemed to me as an imperative form of saying "don't go." But on the insistence of Ole Lehtinen, I agreed that was a misunderstanding and I said, Okay, it is a Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. misunderstanding. I -- in the meantime I put my critical remarks of the way the interview was conducted and I insisted on having the interview transcript, because without that I couldn't do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact you asked for -- you had your meeting with the Defence on the 17th of June, 2004. And the following day you asked Mr. Lehtinen for your transcript of your OTP interview. Isn't that right? It was the day of your interview with the Defence. On the 18th of June, 2004, you asked for your transcript. Right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a rather long question, so I don't understand -- I don't seem to recollect the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let me just put it -- does it sound right to you that it -- it was -- your interview with the Defence was on the 17th of June, 2004? Does that date sound right to you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be that date, although I don't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And was it the day after your interview when you asked -- you met with Mr. Lehtinen and you complained about not having your -- the transcript of your interview and you asked him for it? Was it the day after your interview with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was on the next day when I made known my remarks about the way of the contacts we were having with Ole Lehtinen and the absence of the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And isn't it the case that four days later you were -- Mr. Lehtinen gave you the five CDs that contained your recorded interview and your prior testimony in the Milosevic case? Didn't that happen just four days later on the 22nd of June, 2004?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the date. It may have been two, three, or four days, I can't be accurate, when -- after that when I received those five diskettes that were alleged to be the transcript of my statement in the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, you've already told us -- it was your transcript in the Milosevic case and also it was your transcript of your OTP interview; that's what you were told, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what Mr. Lehtinen told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you've already told us that you never went back to Mr. Lehtinen to tell him that you were unable to open those CDs. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't try to open them immediately, but after some time, a rather long time, I tried to open them but it was impossible for me to open them. I didn't try to do that right away because I wasn't that keen on doing that immediately, thinking that the trial wouldn't start very soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you've already testified before the break that when you were unable to open the CDs, you did not go back to Mr. Lehtinen to tell him that you were unable to open them and to ask again for your transcript. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, because I began to create the impression that a game was being played with these transcripts and I didn't go back to Mr. Lehtinen about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's continue, if we could, with the -- your interview with the OTP. I'm going to ask you to turn, please, to page 34 of the Albanian and it's 34 also of the English. On the English it's towards the bottom third of the page -- no, I'm sorry. It's at the top of the page. And on the Albanian on page 34 it's in the middle of the page, and I'm going to play this portion of the interview for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "O.L.: But fighting or not, I'm saying that there have to be a certain kind of structure in the area. I know that already in April 1998 there was regularly weekly meetings in Klecka. Did you join these meetings? "S.B.: Because -- no, because I was not part of the command structure in Klecka. There was occasional -- I would occasionally take part in these meetings, for example in May. So for the most -- the most period -- sorry, the most time during the May I spent staying in Kacanik and Ferizaj. It was due to the fact that I was -- I was engaged in coordinating the whole work with Agim Bajrami, commander Agim Bajrami. My specific task was to -- was to -- was as far as weapons supply was concerned. Right. When I would happen to be there, in Kroimire I'm talking, I would help in things like these bunkers or trenches -- I would rather put it point in Kroimire rather than call it company or battalion or things like that. At that time I -- well, I thought Fatmir Limaj was -- must have -- was a member of General Staff at that time, I thought. But at the end of 1998 I realised that he hadn't been the member of General Staff. Yes. So I was free to put suggestions as to whom, for example, to assign to Petrastica, to deal with Petrastica. Of course my proposals were not always taken into consideration, but I had enough -- I had enough -- let's say contacts with Fatmir. So you'd be -- so as to be free to put forward proposals. And the same way that I thought about Fatmir or allegedly being a member of General Staff, most of the people I know thought the same about me, that I probably was a member of General Staff. "A.W.: Can I" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, in April and May of 1998 you thought that Fatmir Limaj was a member of the General Staff, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have made it clear here that in April and May I was in Kacanik in the other part of the operations and it's something else what I might have thought, after a meeting I had with Fatmir in the April of 1998 during which we discussed political issues. And at that time he left me a good impression of a man with intellectual potential and political expertise. That's why I created impression of him being a member of the General Staff, but that was just my impression; it was not a fact. I explained that I realised later that he became a member of the General Staff at the end. I think it was November/December of 1998 when my brother too became a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, isn't it true that you thought he was a member of the General Staff because during this time period he was the person through whom you would communicate with the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think that was the reason why I created that impression; it was because of his abilities, I think. Because if we were to look at the reality as you are saying, how could I have thought of my own brother as such when he did become a member of the General Staff? It often happened that we thought of each other or of some third person of being in some position when in fact he was not, just because we knew him to be a member of the Presidency of the LPK or General Council of the LPK. So positions were different from reality. And I understood that Fatmir Limaj became a member either in November or in December of 1998. I explained here how people believed that I, too, was a member of the General Staff but in fact they were simple -- merely suppositions of soldiers or some superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And people thought that you were a member of the General Staff because you were exercising a coordinating role in the area that you were organising, as you say here in the interview. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: People may have created the impression which I cannot account for, but I have believed and thought when people have asked me whether I was a member of the General Staff when in fact I was not. Maybe because of the -- of my duty as responsible for the supply of arms and for the actual shipment of these arms or because of the political or military talks I gave to people; maybe this is why they created that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, do you see here in this portion of the interview where you say: "We had not even defined companies or battalions but only posts"? This is -- you're speaking about the time you were in Kroimire. Do you see where you say that?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's true, isn't it, that at that time there were -- there were posts in different villages. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already explained I think this -- the use of the word "point," why I used that word. And I am explaining again. In fact it was the unit of Pjetershtice. If it was called "point" I don't know what it's meaning would be when in fact the unit in Pjetershtice was operating along this Carraleve-Belince line and covered two villages. Today I cannot describe to the Trial Chamber as a point because the form of organisation that existed then was the guerrilla unit which operated in a village or a town and it operated in a horizontal line in its positions. That was the form of organisation then. But the other organisation that is claimed to be as battalion -- in the form of battalions and companies was not in existence at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think you told us earlier that in your mind the word "point" has a special military meaning. Can you explain to us what you understood the word point to mean.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not a special military significance. The word point is translation from a foreign language which I never wanted to accept as authentic expression to be used in my own language. In fact, it was borrowed by the Serb expression, "policijski punkt," something which I never wanted to use because the word point implies a limited existence as a military expression. And as an expression of the Albanian language, which describes better the time when the units operated in a frontal line, is in fact a "frontal line." This is why I never wanted to refer to them as points because at that time the form of organisation irrespective of the interpretations didn't seem to me as points but only as guerrilla units. I already explained that the strategy of the General Staff was the horizontal spread of the guerrilla units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it still your testimony that the reason you used the word point in your interview here is because of propaganda that you had heard? Is that still your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course it is because the description of this period has been constantly done using the word point and this word has affected also me. That's why I have used the word point. It's the fact of the propaganda and agitation then by the war waged of the KLA and which has often accounted for not given a truthful description of its real organisation. This is the reason why.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And here when you say you that had support -- when you were surveying positions, bunkers, and other things, you had support from Fatmir. You're talking about your time in Kroimire. You had support from Fatmir. Can you tell us what kind of support you had from Fatmir?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can. The positions, the trenches, and the bunkers began to be dug sometime in the middle of June and were continued constantly. When I mentioned the support of Fatmir I meant both, materielly and observing, supervising, these positions, whether everything was okay, whether the trench was dug properly. I meant that we talked about these issues. We helped each other as co-fighters. I have also pointed out the support we got from the General Staff to operate in this regard, that is to dig trenches and to build bunkers. I have already I think clearly explained that that was a combined war, a war that was unprecedented until then. It was a war waged through guerrilla units positions, something which had never happened until then. The General Staff supported this kind of warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, you're aware that there was fighting in Carraleve starting on the 14th of June, 1998. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date of the fighting this Carraleve, but I know that there was fighting in June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Approximately in the middle of June. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say mid-June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the trenches were already dug by then, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were fighting going on even before the trenches were dug up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But by mid-June when there were serious fights with the Serbs in Carraleve, the trenches were already dug, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The trenches could not be dug within a day. These trenches required a continuous work, a work that continued in June and July. Some trenches were open in the beginning, in Pjetershtice, as the first frontal -- front line. Later on we opened the canal and the bunker. I cannot say when the positions were ready for a fight to defend Carraleve. What I can say is there was work going on in June and July regarding the opening of trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did Fatmir Limaj come to Kroimire or Petrastica or Carraleve to super -- to observe, supervise, the positions and see if everything was okay?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that Fatmir Limaj was at the bunkers and trenches at that time, but I know that Fatmir Limaj visited me especially in July in Kroimire. There was a visit that we paid together in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blinaje National Park. Simply, in July I had frequent contacts with Fatmir Limaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you've testified that when you -- what you meant by support from Fatmir when you were doing the trenches and bunkers in Kroimire was that -- you said "I meant both materielly and observing, supervising these positions, whether everything was okay, whether the trench was dug properly." And my question is: Did he come to Kroimire in order to do that, to give that kind of support?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the form you're putting it, it wasn't so. He came on a visit in Blinaje, as I said earlier, and during this visit of course we went out to the positions lying along the Magura-Shale road above Laletic village, and up to the village which name I cannot remember at the moment. So it was Laletic, Blinaje, and I don't remember the name but there is a village nearby. These are the villages where our positions were. If he had any remarks, he would tell me what would be a better solution and it was up to me to decide whether to accept or not to accept his advice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when was this? Was this in July?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in late June/beginning of July. It is very difficult for me to remember these issues correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it before or after you were appointed to the Nerodimlje zone, to this -- to the subzone of Nerodimlje, to be the commander of the subzone of Nerodimlje, was it before or after?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember whether it was before or after, but surely it was within the same period of time when I had received instructions to operate from the General Staff concretely from Jakup Krasniqi to coordinate the units in Lipjan municipality. More frequent contacts we had after July when I was appointed the commander of the zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is it your testimony now that Fatmir Limaj didn't give you any support with respect to trenches and bunkers in -- being built in Kroimire or Petrastica or Carraleve?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I -- we did not open trenches in Kroimire but the trenches were mainly along Carraleve. They were in Zborce and in the front line of Blinaje. Fatmir helped me with his advice, and of course he helped me in materials which were required by the soldiers and which I didn't have. I mean here pickses [as interpreted] and spades. So he would advise me what would be the better solution; this is what we discussed. You should bear in mind that there were two ways of opening trenches. Some preferred zigzag trenches and some trenches in a straight line. So these were our discussions, what would be the better way to open the trenches, whether in a zigzag or in a straight line. So I took his advice and I acted the way I thought it was for the best.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But did he give you any support for the trenches in Carraleve? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that Fatmir was in Carraleve when the trenches and bunkers were opened. I know that he came for a visit in Kroimire and I know that we visited together the national park in Blinaje because he wanted to see this park that he hadn't seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And then you say that -- you say that -- that you were able to say that a person should be established, for example, at Petrastica who would command that post, a person who should be set up. And you said -- and then you say: "Often they did not -- they did not accept my proposal but I made the proposals." And my question is: Who did you make the proposals to?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I made these proposals to the unit that was there and I thought that I knew better the acts of soldiers who were members of that unit. In Petrastica this opportunity was taken away from me and -- my proposal as well, as was the case with Zborce.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to move on in the transcript because there's further discussion about these issues and the structure. And it's -- on the Albanian it's page 35; on the English it's -- continues on page 34 where the last one left off. And on page 35 it's -- on the Albanian transcript it's in -- it's in the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think we need to switch to the Sanction. I'm not getting any sound --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "A.C.: End of April" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: "A.C.: Approximately? "THE INTERPRETER: End of April? "A.C.: End of April 1998? "S.B.: I don't know whether it was end of April or beginning of May. It must have been a unit made up of eight or ten people in Kroimire. "A.C.: And you were the commander in Kroimire at that time, the organiser? "S.B.: Yeah -- well, I don't know whether it was -- as I said end of April or beginning of May, I was in Kacanik at that time. And on my return from Kacanik I brought along also weapons. So we were placed in Kroimire. So I found their soldiers coming from abroad. There were three or four soldiers coming from abroad. There were people from Kroimire as well. So these people would distribute weapons to the persons they considered suitable to do the job. And as a matter of -- as a course of a normal procedure, I got in touch with Fatmir. So I asked Fatmir what our job was supposed to be in Kroimire and where to -- how to proceed. "A.C.: So who's in charge in Kroimire at this time? You are? "S.B.: There were two persons in charge at that time, so I wouldn't -- I wouldn't know how -- who was number one. "A.C.: So who was it? You and who else? "S.B.: It was me and Luan, Ramiz Qeriqi. "A.C.: So you and Luan were in charge in Kroimire at the end of April 1998? "S.B.: Well, end of April or beginning of May. "A.C.: And Fatmir Limaj dealt directly either with you or Luan at that time? "S.B.: Well, I want also to clarify something here. I wasn't able to take as many decisions as possible because I didn't know people." "A.C.: Sorry, I wasn't actually asking that. Fatmir Limaj dealt either with you or Luan at the end of April, beginning of May 1998? "S.B.: Yes. "A.C.: And Fatmir Limaj was dealing with the KLA Main Staff, wherever that was? "S.B.: Yes, he was a coordinator of this job. "A.C.: So here we have a structure. We have the KLA Main Staff at the top, Fatmir Limaj underneath, and you and Luan underneath Fatmir Limaj. Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Shall I ask him once again to clarify to explain him better how did you put it? "A.C.: What I want to just say is what you've outlined to me is the basic structure: KLA Main Staff at the top; underneath, Fatmir Limaj in Klecka; and then underneath you and Luan in Kroimire. That's what you just said. Correct? "S.B.: It was a different -- it was a different nature of things that I and Luan used to deal with, so we were different in what we were doing. Me and Luan. "A.C.: Yeah, but let's go back to the question. I'm not interested in what you and Luan were doing. I just want you to confirm that at this time, at the end of April of 1998, there was a rudimentary military structure: KLA Main Staff, Fatmir Limaj taking instructions from them, and then you and Luan in Krajmirovce taking instructions from Fatmir Limaj. Correct? "S.B.: Yeah, that's correct. I just wanted to clarify that. "A.C.: Yeah, that's fine. Thank you. "O.L.: And at this" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Buja, I want to take this passage point by point, the important points. You said at the beginning of this passage in the interview that when you came to Kroimire there were some other soldiers who had come from abroad and who had begun to set up in Kroimire, and that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I didn't get an interpretation of what you just said.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter couldn't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I could go through this passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you ask your question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Partway through this passage at the beginning you say that when you came to Kroimire you found some -- you found some soldiers there who had come from abroad who also belonged to Kroimire. And there you're referring to Ramiz Qeriqi and another soldier. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SHUKRI BUJA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the month must have been mistaken because this happened in May and not in April. It was in May when I contacted with these soldiers after my return from Kacanik and when I brought the first weapons supply. I found there three or four soldiers, I'm not quite sure, who were from Kroimire. In the beginning of my testimony here I stated that I knew or that Luan introduced himself to me and another soldier, who was Fadil, and there were other soldiers, as it is said here, who were from the village of Kroimire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And in fact you do say in the interview here that it's at the beginning of May or end of April when you bring the weapons to Kroimire from Kacanik. And you say that you distributed the weapons to the people that they thought would be the best KLA soldiers. And then you say: "I -- usually in contact with Fatmir, that is I asked where we should set up and what operations we should carry out since we were in Kroimire." And then you say: "I asked Fatmir what we should do." That's what happened, isn't it?
